utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, we will be able to conclude this witness's testimony today? That's a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm confident -- hopeful that we can, and I think we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you may read the declaration to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may have a seat. You may begin, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll just wait a moment while they adjust his seat, Your Honour, or do you want me to begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the seat be adjusted first, and he should be brought closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Nurko Dervisevic, born on the 25th of May, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many years did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Seven years. Four elementary school and three occupational school. I studied to become a joiner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And were you born and raised in the municipality of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was born there, and I spent my entire life there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dervisevic, I'm going to ask you some questions about some statements that you gave to the ICTY investigators, if I may ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Just related to protective measures for this witness. No measures. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I never requested measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't arise. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember giving a statement to ICTY investigators in February of 1998?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you also remember giving another statement in April of 2008 in which you made some corrections to your 1998 statement? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I didn't go through every single detail, but I think I corrected a lot of mistakes that were there in terms of place, names, people's names and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you've come to The Hague in the last couple of days, have these two statements been read to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lady who proofed me for my appearance, and we checked the statement for veracity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And we did make a couple of additional changes --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's too loud?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: A little softer, please. It's too loud. The sound is very loud, and I don't like noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll try to speak a little softer. Now, we made a couple of more changes to your 1998 statement, and I'm going to ask you about those little changes in a minute, but other than those changes everything else in the statement is still true; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May we bring up -- it doesn't have a 65 ter number. It's the statement, 1998 statement, ERN 00584654 to 4669. I would like to go to page 2 in both versions, and it's second paragraph down on the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In just a moment, sir, you'll see your statement come up on the screen, and then I'm going to ask you a question. Okay. Now, sir, on the left side of your screen, do you see part of your statement in the Bosnian language? On the left side of the screen. Is that yes?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you see that -- in the statement you say the date of your arrest was 9 of June of 1992. Now, would you like to change that date?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this is a small inaccuracy. It was sometime in June. The 9th, the 19th. I tend to get confused about dates. It might have been the 19th. Maybe it was recorded as the 9th, but I'm actually quite certain that it was the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, also in this statement when we read down a little bit further, you talk about the badges that were on the Serb police or army persons who took you into custody, and you describe an SDS badge with two eagles and also a three-coloured flag. Now, would you like to make a correction to that?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: In the barracks there was an SDS flag. The sign belonged to the SDS, and then the two eagles and the cross, that was for the whole thing. It was some sort of a formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But with particular focus on what these men were wearing, you told me that you -- it was not possible that two badges be together. Didn't you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that could have been the case, not two at the same time. There were several signs, different signs that were turning up, and there were these radical parties with two eagles and a cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I just want you to focus on the badge. Can you remember, sitting here today, what -- what badges these men were wearing, and if you can, would you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: The civilians, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: The civilians weren't wearing anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. Just the two -- the Serb police or army that arrested you in June of 1992. Do you remember the emblems? Okay. Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: The people who arrested me had something blue on them. The car said "Police," and the insignia belonged to the SDS, if I remember correctly. They were members of the SDS. It was a party symbol.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I would like to go to page 7 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. In the B/C/S, it's the last paragraph on the page. In English, it's the first paragraph. Sir, I'd like you to take a look, again, on the left side of the screen and look at the last paragraph, the first sentence. It says that you saw Milan Lukic take away more than 20 people. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I heard his voice, but there were five or six persons involved. I don't think he could have handled this on his own. As for mistreatment, he was the one who came most frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I'll ask you about that in a minute, but my question is, with reference to this, you did not actually see Mr. Lukic do this, did you?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It was night-time. It was dark. I didn't know what time it was. All the people who did that, I couldn't see them, but I heard voices and I recognised the voices --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: -- because he came several times and I saw him personally. I met him then. I hadn't known him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So I asked you a minute ago, other than these corrections to your statement, everything else is still true; is that -- to the best of your knowledge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The indictees themselves should tell us whether it was like this or not. I think they should be free to say what they have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this witness's 1998 and 2008 statement be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, just some more questions, sir. In 1992 were you a member of any army?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And were you ever a member of any army?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In June -- okay. In June of 1992, did you wear any type of military clothing at all?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I was a civilian throughout. Normally, I would wear a jacket such as the one I'm wearing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you carry a firearm or any other type of weapon in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No. I never owned a weapon. I hated weapons. I hated even to look at a weapon. I would have thrown it away. I never carried a weapon, and if someone can prove otherwise, they're welcome to have a go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to draw your attention to June of 1992 and ask you, do you recall being arrested or taken into custody at some point?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I was on my way out. There were civilians leaving. I didn't join that convoy. I wasn't able to. My family left on that convoy, my wife and our four children who were underage at that time. I headed down the Rzava river to this village close to Visegrad. The distance may be about one and a half kilometres, and then I came close to this place Boista [phoen] on the Rzava river, on the right-hand river bank. This was day-time. It wasn't night-time. It might have been 9 or 10.00 in the morning. There was this - what should I call it - an ambush or whatever. I stopped right there. There was some weapons. You've got to stop. They said, Cross, and I surrendered. They took me to the MUP building. I handed over my ID. There were these lads over there, soldiers, I suppose. They were drinking a little. They gave me some, so I had some too. It was a bit like that, and then Lukic Milan emerged, and he said, Where are your sons? And then he slapped me over the head, the left side of my head, and that's why I still can't hear. I thought my eardrum --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: -- had been shattered, and that's when I fell down, and then they took me away. They'd probably been ordered to take me away, and that's what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness for that answer. Just one follow-up question on this. Now, you say "they." Were these army men or policemen if you know?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It appears that they were Special Police. The car certainly had a writing on it saying "Police," meaning they were police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at some point you were taken to another facility. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: When I woke up, I was drunk. I looked around myself, and I appeared to be in some sort of warehouse, maybe a military one, maybe not a military warehouse, the JNA in this place called Uzamnica. I saw six persons standing in front of me, and they were all familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May we -- may the court usher please bring up on the screen 65 ter number 178.63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, you said when you woke up you were drunk. Can you tell us what made you drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brandy. I'd downed some outside the MUP building. It was given to me, and I accepted because I was feeling quite depressed. By this time, I would have drank poison if I had been given poison let alone brandy. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that they did anything particular to me, same as though we were in a pub or something, and they gave me some brandy, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, okay. Thank you. Please try to wait for the question, and then you answer the question. Thank you. Okay. Could you look at the picture that's on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic is on his feet here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting. Just one intervene. In transcript, I think that the witness said lines -- page 43, lines 18 and 19, the previous one, from -- from 19 to 21 that he said like a friends, like friends in a pub.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They weren't being unpleasant to me or anything. So after I'd been slapped, they sort of rued that. They felt bad about me. Those people, as far as I remember, never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So I'd ask you to look at the photograph that's on the screen and ask if you can tell us what this photograph is. What's in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: This is Uzamnica. Down here is the JNA barracks, and these are the warehouses. This one over here was the first one. There 's a path there to an outpost, a military outpost --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: -- and that's where we were detained, and this one had three partitions inside, and we were in the mid-section, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the photograph be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the photograph will be admitted as Exhibit P113; and just for the record, the 2008 witness statement with ERN number 0634 through 03947 will be admitted as P112.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the statement of April 2008?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P111.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, may we bring up 65 ter number 178.41, please. Sir, do you recognise the building that is in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: This is the warehouse, the military storage facility for their military equipment, and we were in the mid section. Here is where the women were, and over here, well, we didn't know. We were in no position to know who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So how many months were you in detention at Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-eight months. It was in June that I was detained, and then there was an exchange on the 10th of October at the brotherhood and unity bridge. There were ten of us that got exchanged and eight ladies as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, so for the 28 months that you were detained, were you always in this building?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many other detainees were in the middle section as you described it with you?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Up to 26, and then some people would be taken away, some new people brought in. So this varied, but the maximum, to my knowledge, was 26, perhaps 27. Some only stayed briefly. Some stayed all the way until the exchange took place. Some mothers were taken away. There were some private exchanges going on, as well, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, may --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: There were ten men left and eight women, and that was the final exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the photograph be admitted in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P114.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the ethnicity of the other detainees with which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: All Muslims. In January, when I first -- or rather, the first month I came there, there was among them a man named Pero Gacic from Gorazde. He said he was a member of the Gorazde Territorial Defence. Maybe he was lying to us, but I'm just telling you what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, were there guards guarding the place in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: There were guards, two guards in a group. We were locked up with a chain and padlock, and they were in charge of the prison or guarding, but either they didn't want to or they could not prevent outsiders from coming into the prison and beating people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I just want you to focus right now on the guards, and tell us if you can tell us what they were wearing and if you knew any of them by name.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I know quite a lot of them. Their clothing was blue, but I also saw them in civilian clothes. But if you want me to talk about guards, I'll start -- do you want me to talk about guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to ask you a question about what you recall them wearing. You did name these guards in your statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I can repeat it. Do you want me?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I stand by the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of these guards?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what the living conditions were like at Uzamnica; and by this, I mean food, sleeping conditions, water, bathing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It was a warehouse, not a house, not a hotel. There was hay under the windows and some army blankets we used to cover ourselves, and for 26 people the food could not be sufficient. One loaf of bread was divided into nine pieces. We got tea, some marmalade to spread on bread, and boiled eggs. That was the first month and the second month, and as the number of us decreased, the food increased in amount. We bathed outside the hangar, behind the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell me how much you weighed when you were released from detention?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: 42 what?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I weighed myself in Sarajevo at the exchange, after the exchange. Before detention, I weighed 62 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to direct your attention now to ask about Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic, okay?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Prior to the war, did you know a person by the name of Milan Lukic? That's --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I did not. Maybe he knew me, but I didn't know him. I never knew him before that camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: When was the first time that you met Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: That time when I was taken into custody to the MUP and when he attacked me, slapping me over the head. Maybe I had run into him before the war, but I had never noticed him. I had my own business to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, when you were at the detention facility, did you ever see Milan Lukic there?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic came occasionally. He would beat a couple of people and then tell them, "Now get some rest," and then he would go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you ever beat you?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He pressed me against the pillar in the warehouse, and he kicked me from behind. One time he chased me across the warehouse. He put his foot on my back. When I fell, I tried to crawl forward, and he did the same thing to some other people as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you said you didn't know him before the war, so how did you come to learn that his name was Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It was another man in detention, Saban Muratagic, who told me. I think Milan Lukic is from a village close to his village, Zupa. Milan is from Rujiste. He can confirm that. So this man knew him, and Milan didn't beat that man, and I was wondering why he was spared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did anyone else beat you other than Milan Lukic during your time in detention?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once there was Milan Spasojevic, called Mico, and he took out me and Mustafa Cuprija, a neighbour of mine. He was four years older than I. He gave us some sticks to beat each other with three times each. He hit me three times, and it was very painful, and I hit him three times, but this man, "You're not doing it well enough. You don't want to beat each other?" He took the sticks from us and beat us. This man was sick. He had trouble with his blood sugar, and he was peeing blood. This same Mico --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- now, before the war, did you know a person by the name of Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was an employee of the MUP, the Visegrad station of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you ever see Sredoje Lukic at the Uzamnica detention facility?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I recognised him only once. It was in the later months. It could have been July or perhaps August. He came once when there were few of us. Actually, at that time I was alone in that prison. He came with Milan. And when I saw him with Milan, I was surprised. Sredoje didn't look to me like a man of that kind. He hit me several times, and Milan took that man, Semso Poljo, a retired man from Bijeli Potok who was at that time was over 70, and he took that man away, and again, I stayed alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say, he -- he hit me several times, do you mean Sredoje Lukic hit you several times?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Leading. Leading. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's very leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and Milan took that man and said, "Hit him. Hit him." I don't know how he felt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who beat you several times? Who was it that hit you several times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you saw Milan Lukic at the detention facility, did you see him -- other than beating detainees, did you see him doing anything else?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He probably knew those detainees by name. He called out Enes Dzaferovic and his brother and another young man, Omerovic, the son of Himzo Omerovic, and said, "You are going for the weekend to Bajina Basta," and he took those three men away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you know these three men personally?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And since --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: They're from -- Enes Dzaferovic and his brother lived close to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Whereas Himzo Omerovic's son was from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear from where.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you knew these -- the answer was yes, you knew these three men personally, right? Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us just find out where the son was from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us again, sir, where the son was from?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He was detained with his father. The brothers, fathers, and sons were locked up together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think the question is, do you know what village or municipality they were from?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Visegrad, municipality of Visegrad. But this Omerovic was from Dusce, a suburb of Visegrad where the furniture factory is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, after Milan took out these men, did you -- have you ever seen these men again?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Have you spoken with their family members?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: When I got out and came to Sarajevo, perhaps a year later I ran into his father - because he was a driver for the furniture company Varda - (redacted), and I asked him, "Did your sons come back?" He had heard stories that they were alive, but he said, "Never. Never, Nurko."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you see Milan Lukic take -- no. Don't -- wait for the question, please. Did you see Milan Lukic take other people away?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And on how many occasions did you see this?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He took away -- there were two more occasions after this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you know the people whom he took away?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And have you ever seen any of these people since that time he took them away?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who has ever seen the people whom he took away?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No one has ever said that those people have come back to their families or that they were alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you grew up in the Visegrad area. You said that earlier. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, always. That's the municipality where I was born and where I spent all my life until all this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you know anyone before this happened? Did you know anyone by the name of Milan Lukic, who went by the name Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I know about the guards and the movement of commanders. One only was from Zenica, and the other three guard commanders were from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: None of those guards were called Milan Lukic, were they?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was one Milan Zecevic and Ilija Zecevic. Those two were brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I even know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with the area in Visegrad known as Mahala?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I grew up there. It's a part of Visegrad. Some people say it's a suburb, but it's a town unto itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Nova Mahala and my street was Dobrinska number 6. Perhaps it has been renamed since.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the next question is, are you familiar with an area known as Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: How would I not know it? There's a sports centre with bungalows and catering facilities, a hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend Mr. Dieckmann hasn't found anything in 65 ter submission for this witness related to those questions, previous two questions, Mahala, Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this witness is born and raised in Visegrad and can testify about the area of Visegrad, and I think it's -- it's background information about this witness, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. What would your point be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We must be informed, Your Honour, in submission -- in 65 submission about what will that witness testify, just to know what we have to prepare for cross-examination. If he opens some new topics, we are little bit surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this a new topic? Isn't this in Visegrad? Isn't the area in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, nothing in the statements and in the 65 ter summary is related to those two locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may. I'm not going to ask him about the Pionirska or the Bikavac incidents. I'm simply going to ask him if he knows how long it would take him to drive from one area to the next area, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question may be asked, and Mr. Cepic, if you can persuade us that you're in any way prejudiced, then you may do that, but not now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us how long it would take to drive from the Mahala area to the Bikavac area?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a ten minutes' walk, and by car you don't need more than five minutes. Visegrad is a small municipality. You can drive from one end to another and around it in just half an hour. It had a population of no more than 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at some point during your detention at Uzamnica, did the Red Cross visit the detainees?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: We were registered by the Red Cross a little too late, but after that they continued to care for us, and probably to the extent of their abilities they visited us, sometimes once in 15 days, sometimes once a month or once in two months. They asked us about hygiene, food, general conditions, and we told them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: And one of us was always put forward to emphasise that everything was excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My question -- the next question would be, did you ever tell them about the beatings?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't dare to. Detainees would tell one another, "Shut up. Don't you dare tell them. We'll get more if they hear that we've complained."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I'm going to ask you, if you would, to please look around the courtroom in just a minute and take your time and look at everyone very carefully, and other than myself and Mr. Groome, I ask if you can tell me if you recognise anyone else in this courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Standard objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We note it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the accused, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you recognise anyone by name and, if so, what are their names?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the service of the Tribunal or among the accused? The accused, I know them, both Milan and Sredoje. We can stand up and look each other in the face.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just ask you, sir, to please, for the record -- you have to tell the record because they have to take it down, type it, which one is Milan and which one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the accused who is standing sit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Which one is Milan, and if you can tell us what he is wearing, what colour he is wearing.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He's sitting. Sredoje had just gotten up and sat back down again. He's now wearing glasses; he didn't used to wear them before. And Milan is not even looking at me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you can distinguish between the colour of suits of these two men?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Their jackets are similar. Sredoje has a white shirt and a tie, and Milan has a blue shirt and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: As you're looking at these two men, can you tell me which one is on the left and which one is on the right as you look at them?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Looking from here, Sredoje is on the right and Milan is on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And are these the two men that you saw at the Uzamnica detention camp and, as you testified to, who beat you?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic, and Sredoje I saw only once when he came together with Milan. I hadn't seen Sredoje before. I am saying here without any coercion, and there were no secret conversations. I want to say this forthrightly here, the whole truth and nothing but truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness has identified the accused correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Chamber how -- what kind of physical or emotional or mental injuries did you suffer as a result of your detention and beatings?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Before medical and specialist panels, I was pronounced to have 70-percent invalidity, so they sent me to retirement in Zenica. And when I applied for remuneration on account of being a civilian victim of war, I started receiving some assistance as a former camp inmate and a civilian victim. That's something that they started paying out later on account of damage to my health, et cetera. The canton -- the cantonal authorities provided that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your health was like before 1992?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I was healthy like a bull, one the best workers at the furniture factory. I was the one who best dealt with the strain of night-shifts, and people even wondered how at my age I was so fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, sir, a few more questions. In 1992, did you have any children and, if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I had nine children, six sons and three daughters. Out of those children, two were twins.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And after the war started, did anything happen to any of your sons?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. One of the twins, Samir, was taken away. That's what I heard. At the time when they told me, I couldn't believe it, but I wasn't an eyewitness to that. But I heard that there is a witness, another boy who was then 14 or 15 who was taken away with my son together with another younger boy. I heard that Samir was killed at the Drina Bridge, and I would actually forgive him a lot if I could only get the remains of my son back, but they were never found.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: My child is gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us how old Samir was?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He was not yet 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us who told you that your boy had been taken away and killed at the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: This boy didn't dare tell me for a long time. It was only five or six days after the event that he told the mother - my wife, that is - Samir was killed, it's very hard for me to tell you, and my wife fainted. He told us that he had been taken there and then taken back to the MUP to be interrogated, that Milan killed our boy together with another man and killed Said Herceglic, another worker from my company, and I know all the workers in our company. I don't know that boy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: That man was called Lempa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May we go into closed session for one last question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Jason Alarid, and I represent Milan Lukic. Good morning. Now, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions, and I was unclear about just what you said. You mentioned a gentleman Lempa that was -- worked at the factory. Did you say that --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: The furniture factory. Varda, it was called, Varda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you say that Lempa was killed with your son? Is -- that was your understanding, but I was confused.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: There was this witness who testified about Samir my son, and he said that Said was killed then too. They called him Lenda, but his real name was Said Herceglic, the former employee of the furniture factory. He used to live in Nova Mahala. I can't remember the street, but that was the neighbourhood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How old was Lenda?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1940, and he might have been born sometime around 1936, roughly speaking. He was several years older than me, quite powerfully built. In the basement of his home he used to store some drinks. His wife, Stana, and then he had two sons who were grownups.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can I ask you another question? The boy that told you about --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The boy who told you about your son and Lenda, did he tell you about his stay at the -- at the MUP and what happened to him there? And please tell us what he told you if he did.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He says he was sent back to the MUP building and then he spent some time there. I can't remember what he said, a day or so, and that's where the story ends. He never said he had been beaten. I can't say that. And he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that you lived in Visegrad area your entire life. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: That's true. It was only in the last war, the first war back in 1943, I was a refugee and my family had fled to Vratnik near Sarajevo, and we stayed there until we were able to return to our homes in 1945 when Yugoslavia was free again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And during your -- your life in Visegrad, did you know or hear of Milan Lukic's family, Mile Lukic, his father?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know his father. I know some people from Rujiste. There is a man named Ivanovic Jovan who worked in my department, and he was from there, and I think he said he lived in France for some time, this man named Jovan. And Rujiste, Rujiste -- I know there is a family named Liska. I think they moved to Visegrad at some point. They bought some land or something and built a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: At Rujiste maybe -- there -- there weren't too many people there, not too many households.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by the Prosecutor on direct examination if you knew any other persons by the name of Milan Lukic in the area of Visegrad, and it's my understanding that you said no. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. There is no Milan Lukic in Visegrad itself. It could be one of the other municipalities around. There are names that are similar, but there is no Mile Lukic. Milan Lukic. Milan Krsmanovic. Mile Zecevic. There are some Miles but no Mile Lukic. Milan, Sredoje, and Dragan were the only three Lukics around, Dragan being the youngest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So Lukic itself is not a very common last name, or is it a common name?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Very common. I'm not sure. We might be talking at cross-purposes. Can you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is -- is Lukic a common last name around where you're from?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No, not really. Not in Visegrad municipality. Maybe further afield in another municipality or even republic, but not in Visegrad. Whoever knows many people named Lukic they should perhaps come up and say so. Maybe you mean Lucic. Those are a bit thick on the ground. Yes, that's true, but that's different. That's Lucic. Over at my daughter-in-law's place, there was a worker at one of the local factories. His name was Lucic, but I don't think that particular man named Lucic is in any way related to this Lukic. Maybe it's just mix-up, but we're looking at a Lucic there, and when you talk about Milan, Milan's name is Lukic. It is similar, but then again, it's not quite the same thing and it's not the same family name, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, sir, and I don't mean to interrupt you, but please try and answer my questions a little shorter because I want to get you home today, okay? Now, did you know a Milan Lukic, though, from Turgovaca, about 45 [Realtime transcript read in error, "35"] years old at the time in 1992? Turgovaca?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Turgovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And 45 years old, not 35 as the transcript reads.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No. The place is Glogova. That's one stop away from the railway station. You take a train, and it's the next stop. It might be -- the distance might be a kilometre from those buildings there, and that's on the right-hand riverbank of the Rzava. Glogova, I don't know. Also, maybe a correction. Dubrava, the place was Dobruna. I made that correction there, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, I don't mean to interrupt you. So you don't know a Milan Lukic, 45 years old. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, sir when you were detained at the Uzamnica barracks, did police bring --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anyone else aside from the person I met at the camp, Milan Lukic or Lukic Milan. Lucic, yes. There were many of those around, but that was Lucic and this is Lukic and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody might get these two mixed up, but then we have to know what is what.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were there in the barracks, when you were detained there, is it true that police would bring the new detainees to the prison?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Can I just please get the volume up because I can't hear properly. It's very low now. Just the tiniest bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is that better, sir?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: A little bit more, please. Yes, this is fine now. Please go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, during your stay there -- you were there for 28 months, correct?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And your last day there was October 1994, in there somewhere?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so during your 28 months there, did you see police bring new detainees and take new -- and old detainees away?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Two people would be brought in at a time, for example, and then there was this military warehouse, and we couldn't see who it was that they were bringing. They would just throw the person inside, slam the door shut, and that was that. It's not like we could actually see much. I can't really say. But new people kept arriving all the time, and some people had been taken away. Actually, new people being brought there. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it true that sometimes those people would be taken away to the police station for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I myself was interrogated at the barracks. There was Ramiz Kulo. There was me, Muharem Samardzic, and Adem Beberovic, over at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were interrogate --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: But I don't know about the MUP building. I wasn't taken there for interrogation. Was anyone else? I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, before you were in the prison and before you were arrested, you worked at the Varda factory, correct?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, the furniture factory --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: -- I was a joiner working with joinery machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you tell us when your last day at the factory was, your last day of work?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: The salaries were distributed. It was payroll day, maybe the 1st of June, the 2nd of June, the May salaries; and then in my department I was the only Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And your last day of work, if it was the May salaries paid June 1st, is it true that you were arrested on the 9th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has already testified to what he believed the date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm simply going off the statement, which was admitted under the 92.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Then you should -- I would suggest that he ask about the statement because in his direct testimony that's not what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please clarify because your statement says you were arrested specifically on the 9th of June, 1992. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that might be the day of my arrest, or the 19th. I'm not sure about the date, but I'm sure about the month. It was June. But I'm not exactly positive, and I can't say, but the -- I think no later than the 19th of June. Maybe it was my mistake. Maybe I said the 9th at the time, and maybe I said the 19th and it was simply misrecorded. You know, errors can always occur because I did personally correct some of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now -- now, the one other --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Don't hold it against me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I do not, sir. One the other things that I'd like to ask you, though, is -- is because you indicate that before you were arrested you put your family on a convoy, and so I'm just trying to figure out, how long before you were arrested did you put your family on a convoy? And I'd ask you to name the members of your family at that went on the convoy, please.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Four of my children and my wife and my two daughters-in-law, and then maybe there was another lady neighbour of mine. They went to the Red Cross, and then I was there at the Rzava river, and I wasn't allowed to get onto that convoy. I heard that people were getting off the convoy; I have no idea why, and then I started working down the Rzava river in order to reach a village called Okrugla because that was probably where the convoy stopped, and then the civilians assembled there in a bid to go through the woods and reach Gorazde. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you remember simply the date of the convoy, and maybe referring to how long after your last day of work was the convoy.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Some left before my family left. Where they left for is not something that I can say. It was something that was organised by the Red Cross, the convoys. There were just regular lorries, sometimes buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir. Sir --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: And then my wife told me when I came eventually that they had been put on a lorry. Luga [phoen] Gladanac was the driver and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell me why your twin sons were not on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well -- well, they couldn't leave because it was taken away. He never got to the convoy. Only those that survived left on that convoy. My wife, my youngest daughter, and three sons, Almir, Dervis, and Enes. Enes was my youngest child, youngest male child. And they were married, the two elder daughters, and then the oldest son was somewhere -- or, rather, along the front line, Crni Vrh or someplace like that, and then my two eldest sons, they were elsewhere engaged in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you're saying today that Almir was on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Someone caught him. He was taken to the MUP building but they released him. He said, I have a farm; I have to go and feed my cattle; it's under a half kilometre from the town itself; and then after working hours I have to go there; I have to provide for my family, financially, I mean, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you were exchanged from the -- ultimately, you were part of an exchange from the Uzamnica barracks. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: The barracks, those of us who were there, they assembled us, and then further down some other people joined --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: -- I don't know, and then they took us -- I don't know where we were taken through exactly because this was night-time. I couldn't follow the route, and then at the entrance we spent the night there, and then they took as far as the Vrbanja bridge, and there was this exchange with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please try to make your answers as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, well. Wouldn't I like that, as well, but I need to explain. I need to make it clear, and then you'll understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, sir, isn't it true that some people that were taken away from the Uzamnica barracks were taken away as part of exchanges?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: There was a private exchange. This was not the regular Red Cross exchange or organised by UNPROFOR, the United Nations, or whoever was in charge of organising those. Hasan Balic was exchanged, and Ahmet Pergirudina [phoen] and Ilijas Cuprija. It's like they were exchanged for some women. Hajrudin, I saw at Visoko. Ilijas, I saw later on twice. He was arrested. I saw him in detention and then after that, once in Sarajevo when we came there. And Hasim Balic, well, quite probably at the time he was -- he left or something. I don't know. I didn't see him, really, and then there was another exchange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And isn't it true that on the day you were arrested, you were brought to the police station along with many other men that day by police who were arresting Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there probably were a couple of people, not that I saw them myself, because this incident outside the station at the door or itself, that's something that I experienced myself, Lukic slapping me. I was brought there by Todorovic Nebojsa and Popovic Goran, and they took me from there all the way out to the military warehouse, the one that you saw with the three doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at the time of your arrest your two eldest sons were --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I saw. If I didn't see something, I say it clearly I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just for the record, the transcript did not get the last part of my question, which is at the time of your arrest your two eldest sons were fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, at the time that you were arrested was the first time that you --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: In May. In May. The war began in May. There were houses burning up in the hills, and then the MUP broke up. How should I put it? People left, and then there was a lot of friction. There were civilians. People were fleeing. Some people were arrested, and some people left. This all began in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you do indicate that you noticed Milan Lukic coming occasionally except for an 8-month period. Can you tell us what that 8-month period was?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know how long that period was. For quite some time he wouldn't turn up. When did he turn up, there was this once he brought a pistol. He stood in front of me. I didn't know if he wanted to kill me or to protect me, and then the commander tried to protect me, and he said, Well, kill me but don't kill him. It's like something was totally wrong there. I can't really complain -- I'm not complaining about the specific people. I'm just complaining about the events, about what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if I were to tell you that Milan Lukic was in gaol from February 1993 through July 1994, would that help orientate you?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and answer that one. In 1993, Guso Ramo and Gojak Ahmo were brought. Gojak Ahmo was not from my municipality. He was from Prijepolje, and Guso Ramo was from my municipality. He was an employee of Varda, and he lived over at Banpolje. Gojak -- what did you say? You were saying something about us being together in prison in Belgrade, and he said, No, I never said that. Well, there you go. That's what Almir said, and that's as much as he said, and then Ahmo said, Okay, if you -- 2.000. He gave him 2.000 marks to Milan to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to let him live, and then there were other people from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we take the adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could please fix my headset. It's falling off my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like it to be tighter. Yes. It was loose. Thank you. It's good now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, before we left, you know, one of the things I was trying to get an exact answer on or as exact an answer as you can give, is the date that you put your family -- I need to know the date you put your family onto the convoy. And even if you can't remember the date, if you could tell me in relation to your last day of work or maybe how many days before you were arrested or something that can help us understand the exact date of that convoy. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It seems it was the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you took your family, including Almir, to the convoy on --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: My wife remembers everything better than I do. She can tell you the hour, if necessary. I should have taken her with me. I think it was the beginning of June. I can't remember the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you remember how many days before the date of your arrest that was?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they left with the convoy, and from that time on I went up the river where my feet took me. I didn't dare to go with them on the convoy because I heard people being taken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you were arrested, is it true that the soldiers had signs of the SDS on them?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it true --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Most of them, they elected that party, that democratic party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, is it true that the police that arrested you had sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It was automatic weapons, not ordinary weapons, but those automatic weapons were of varying calibre. They were automatic, but I could not distinguish because I was never familiar with weapons. I never served in the army, and I never got a weapon myself. An automatic rifle is better than an ordinary rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to tell you in your statement in 1998 you indicated that the men arrested you had sniper rifles, would that help -- would you defer to your statement?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Once at the barracks, this Dragan said it has this thing on top so you can see far and clearly. I was never able to distinguish between weapons myself because I never handled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Dragan who, sir?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Popovic, the one who captured me, and Nebojsa Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And so that is -- that is the person that you were arrested by, correct?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those two arrested me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And these -- and these rifles had a telescopic sight, correct?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It had something like a small mirror. You look into it, and far away things seem much closer up. You can hit anyone. If that's what a sniper is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your statement you indicated that they had camouflage uniforms, but you couldn't tell if they were army or police. Could you tell me the colour of the camouflage?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: One group was in blue uniforms, not light blue, and another group was in camouflage. I cannot tell you very exactly now, but the blueish uniforms were the kind of blue like my shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you first saw Milan Lukic, isn't it true that he was wearing a blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Whether it was their blue police colour, yes. He wasn't wearing a camouflage uniform. He was wearing what looked like a police uniform, not a camouflage one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you would see him at other times, did he have a blue police uniform on?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes he wore even a tracksuit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, before you were captured, when did the aggression start between the SDS and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It could be the end of May. I don't know which day. The army of the Uzice Corps left in the end of May, and after their departure those so-called Eagles came to the company in some sort of uniform, although some were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it true that the Uzice Corps came to disarm the Muslim people and help the SDS take control of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't clear to us, for instance -- I asked one of the soldiers of the corps why the corps had come, and he said to protect the dam from Alija's extremists. Somebody might close the dam and cause a flood. But they did not act in a hostile manner. Shells were falling, people dispersed, and this man said to me, "We are not touching civilians." There were very few people, and they said people can return to work. I did go back to work in order not to lose my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it -- isn't it true that during this time the Uzice Corps were there they plundered the goods -- completely plundered the goods of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the corps. The corps did not take anything. They were just there to stabilise peace. They had suspicions that something might happen. So when we went to work, we would encounter these three men from the corps. We would pass through and then come to a point where we would have to show our IDs, and on the way back another group might check our IDs. They did not act in any hostile manner. According to some sort of agreement, they had to leave; and after their departure, chaos returned. These Eagles came. Who they were, I have no clue. When I asked other people, they said they were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember giving a statement on the 23rd of December, 1994, after your release from the Uzamnica barracks?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Later I gave some statements in Nedzarici when some lawyers, people from the court came. I don't know their exact profession. I gave them the lists of people I made, people who had been in the camp and who had been taken away. No one knows where. A few people were exchanged, and ten --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: -- remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you recall in that 1994 statement indicating that Medo Smajic and his wife as well as Safet Cavkusic and his wife were killed by the Uzice Corps as well as others?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I did not give that particular statement, and I am not familiar with their killing. I know about Smajic, the employee of Varda. When his son came to work, he said, "You say there are no killings, but I found my mother and father dead." And a woman from Donja Mahala said Safet Cavkusic and his wife were killed in their own home. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, is it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to interrupt the flow, but if -- since Defence counsel to going to refer to a prior statement it would be helpful if he directs my attention to that section because the way I read the statement, he didn't say anything about the Uzice Corps killing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Page -- page -- page 3 of the December 23rd statement, middle paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. Ms. Sartorio is right. You must direct us to the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And we could even upload -- bring up 1D10-1916. The B/C/S version is 1D10-1925. It's page 3, middle paragraph; and on the B/C/S version, I'm not quite sure to be honest. It would be top third of page 2, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It's scrolling too fast. I can't ... I think this date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you -- and you did give this statement in 1994 after your release?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: This part which I'm seeing right now, when the water was released, it says here in April, the water level increased and people left for Gorazde. Later, little by little people came back, but when they left again some never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now -- now, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is talking to the side of the microphone. If he could please lean back in his chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, sir can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you a couple of other questions, please. In your statement, a little bit earlier on page 2 of the English version, you say: "I also know that Serbs in Visegrad were armed and that the SDS with its Crisis Staff armed them." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think people had weapons. Maybe individuals had one or two, but those people were very well armed, and it couldn't have been any other weapons than those provided by the army. If you ask me about this, I have an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have about ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know the members of the Crisis Staff in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: You mean soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The SDS.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Visegrad most of them were members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: It was a party that they established, I believe. It was called SDS, and all of them in the Visegrad municipality were members of that party. I don't know that they had any other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did the SDS extremists push the violence against the Muslims in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: As I heard, they raised fears and encouraged the building of bunkers. They said there was a threat. I don't know why, why they needed to sow discord among people. I suppose they didn't like that Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed its independence. I wasn't there to see who clashed with whom. I didn't see it, and I don't know how all this started. When the corps left, it was then that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: One more question. Are you certain that it's Milan Lukic that came to you in September of 1993 and beat you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only me. He beat a number of other people, and he kicked me. He had trainers on his feet when he kicked me and pressed me to the floor with his foot. It was not only once, it was several times. He beat other people and tortured them much worse than he did me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Dervisevic.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My name is Jens Dieckmann. I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic, and I have just a few number of questions to you, and --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: May you be greeted. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: In my questions, I will try to be as short and precise as possible, and I would really appreciate if you also could try to be precise and short so that you could finish for all of us as soon as possible. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Before I start, please let me offer you condolences for your children lost in the war and behalf of the whole Defence team, and we are well aware of the pain and suffer you have gone through, and when I put my questions to you I will do it with all respect to your situation.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Witness, in the course of the further questions, I would highly appreciate if you and myself just use the first numbers of this person and do not call them by their names. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So if I refer to the person in the first line, I will call this person VG-25. And if you refer to this person, I would be grateful if you could also say VG-25.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dervisevic, do you know VG-25?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: VG-25 was together with you in the Uzamnica camp?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Now, do you remember how many months you have been together there?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Five or six months, not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Is it perhaps even possible for you to remember the specific time period, from which month and which year to the other month?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm sorry. It could be -- it was in the summer period, maybe August. Yes, he was there, and he was sent to be exchanged. He was there for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So he arrives there in the summer 1992?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know VG-3?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And again I ask you, have you been together with him in the Uzamnica camp?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He even survived to the exchange when we were exchanged together on the 10th of October. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And could you also specify how many months you have been together in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He was captured in June, and he was with us all the time. He had been brought wounded. His leg was bandaged. I think he was wounded. How, I don't know. Maybe he was a fighting man of Ahmet Sejdic. Those first two were fighting men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Is it June 1992 that he has been brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I don't think July has passed. I can't be exact to a day, but the rest is all accurate. I guarantee for that. It's just the dates that I am not sure about. Both of them are still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You have said that VG-3 was with you all the time. What -- what do you mean by this? Does it mean that he was with you together up to 1994?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And at least I would like to ask you the same questions regarding VG-8. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And he arrived also in summer '92 or later?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: August, '92, late anyway. You see, I said about '93, how they brought Ramo Guso and Ahmo Gojak. Ramo Guso is from our municipality, from Banpolje.
