And then he said all those houses up there in the hill were abandoned, those Serbs there. People would go and pick up some fruit to eat. Yeah, so he survived. He's very thin, very thin and blonde.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm very grateful. Thank you very much. All of you have been -- or have been forced to live together in one hangar, in one barrack? Is it true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: We were all in one hangar. That's what some people called them, but these were military warehouses and storage facilities. We were all in one of those. You saw that in the photograph with the door. We were in the middle section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So you have had the opportunity to realise that when something happened to one of you, the other realised what happened to him. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think the question doesn't make -- isn't clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So when you live together in one room, you have had the opportunity to see if something happened to one of you. If one of you has been mistreated or beaten, the other ones notices this. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's as long as it's something happening in this prison, but we didn't know about anything else. For example, some -- somebody was taken away and we knew nothing about that. The door slams shut. They take him somewhere. If he's still alive, maybe he'll get in touch. He is no longer alive, okay, those who are in the know should say so. There are just these two persons who were brought in 1993. They were there for, how long, maybe up to two months, Guso Ramo and Gojak Ahmo. That's as far as I know. All the time -- well, actually whoever was there had to be in that warehouse, and some people were taken away, and then the exchange came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question to this topics. Is it fair to say that in comparison to the other three people that you have spent the longest time in Uzamnica camp? Have you spent there the longest time from you four with 28 months?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have documents showing that. Were there other camps elsewhere? No, not in Visegrad municipality. Maybe there was that school building or whatever else they're saying, people being locked up, but this was a real military camp, the warehouse, and that's all I know about. I don't know about elsewhere. I'm telling you about what I went through and the people who were there. How on earth am I supposed to know what happened elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Dervisevic, you know Sredoje Lukic? You know Sredoje Lukic before the war?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's that man over there on the right. I know him. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you. In the document tendered into evidence as P112, you said that you know -- knew him approximately 15 years before the war as a policeman in Visegrad. Is it true? Is it is it your statement that you know him such a long time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, could we have the reference in the statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is -- I'm sorry. Is this page 2 of this document, and it's from -- from the -- from the bottom one, two, three four -- the fifth from the bottom. I can read it out. "I had known Sredoje Lukic for approximately 15 years prior to 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This is correct? This is your statement, that you know Sredoje Lukic for such a long time?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He worked there. He had a permanent job at the time there. We would see each other in the Mirzalem [phoen] pub, and they would have drinks and that sort of thing. He knows me better than I know him. Yes. Yes. We simply know each other. He had a job there, and I worked in the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: If you think back to this time before the war, what colour of hair -- what colour has -- the hair of Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic has brown hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you, sir. Mr. Witness, I put it to you that Sredoje Lukic never mistreated or beat you in the Uzamnica camp during the time you have been there. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I know him. He only came once with Milan, the two of them. I was alone, and another man was brought over who was over 70 years of age known as Poljo Semso. Milan beat him. He slapped me a couple of times, and then that man was taken away, and I remained alone in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you very much. I would ask the Court usher to call up the document. I'm sorry. I don't know if the other Defence team tendered the statement from 1994 into evidence, so I would call our Defence number. I would ask the court usher to call 2D01-0288. It is an interview to the Ministry of Interior, Visoko department, from the 23rd December, 1994. And I would ask to go to the page -- to page 5 in the B/C/S version. Mr. Witness, in this interview you have had the opportunity to give all names of victims or perpetrators you have been aware of and you know, correct?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I named the people. When I gave statements, I named the people who went through the camp, some people who were exchanged privately, and then the people who came there for an exchange, and the rest I simply don't know about. Some people were taken away, and I have no idea what became of them, and I don't know who does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. And isn't it true that this statement was done just two months after your release from the Uzamnica camp, roughly?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't have made this statement. We used nothing in the camp. There was no music, no letters, no newspapers, no -- I think that is nonsense. It was later, after the camp, after my stay at the camp, and then I remember later because those people who went missing from Visegrad municipality, they were no longer there, but I knew about that, and I wrote down the names, and may somebody tell me I didn't. I know what I know, and I'll say what I know. About 60 people --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you have a look to the screen in front you and look on the left side of the screen, is it your signature you can see on the left side?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: There, right there. Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you have been aware that with this signature you declared that this statement is the truth and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And isn't it true that you did not mention Sredoje Lukic in this statement done two months after your release at all? You didn't mention him at all in this statement? Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I may have left his name out because he was there once. I may have left that out. Let me just have a look and see if this is the list that I provided in my statement. It's possible that I left something out but -- well, he was there. He can tell you himself. He can look me in the eye and say he came that once and Milan brought him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: And then we know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: May I tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit number 2D15, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: May I now ask the court usher to bring up the document 2D01-0707. This is the second interview to Ministry of Interior, Visoko department, from 6 January 1995.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They called me to the MUP in Visoko, and then I told them what I knew. And then when I came back to Sarajevo, this was given to the United -- the Nedzarici FCOC or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to page 5 of the B/C/S version. Is it already down? Oh, sorry. Sir, again, is it on the left side of the screen, is it your signature on the statement from the 6 January 1995?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And isn't it true that you did not mention Sredoje at all, also, in this statement from the 6th January, 1995, being asked questions about your situation in the camp during the last month?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I left him out. I'm just telling you what happened, and I stated that on the record to the best of my ability. He came once, that once. I did see him. Milan slapped me, slapped Semso, and then this man was with them. There was something going on there, and then I was left alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we also tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit number 2D16, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could the court usher please call up the document 2D01-0728. This is the witness interview to Ministry of Security, Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the 22nd of June, 2007. And it must also be the fifth -- page 5 of the B/C/S version. Perhaps could you scroll down to the end. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you identify your signature under this document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: There, right there. It's printed right there. I wrote this, but my hands were shaking at the time, and I couldn't do any better than this. And then over time, my hand became steadier. Given my condition at the time, even this was a decent job, and I have to use my glasses to do this, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness. Isn't it true that also in this interview you had had the opportunity to give all names of victims and perpetrators you have been aware of and you know during the time you have had in the Uzamnica camp? Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I have a brochure about that. I keep it in my home, but I have it on me right now just in case, and I have my papers, documents showing that I was a victim of war. If you want me to, I can bring that to you. You want me to count this, but one thing I can tell you for sure is that I have a list of those people who were in that camp. Maybe some people were taken away. Maybe someone is alive somewhere out there --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm very well aware. Thank you very much. I'm very well aware what you have suffered during this time. Thank you. Thank you very much. But again, sir, isn't it true that also in this third statement from 2007, you did not mention Sredoje at all regarding the situation in Uzamnica camp during the time you have been there?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I think I did mention him. Why would I mention Milan and not Sredoje if that's how it happened? I don't know. You're asking me this. Is there another man named Lukic? I don't know. I know there are plenty named Lucic, but I don't think so. You know, mistakes are always possible. People leave stuff out, you know, but that's what I'm looking at, and this is what I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you. Thank you very much. Sir, today you have been asked by the Prosecution, and I refer to page 49, line 10 up to 17, and I may quote: "Did anyone else beat you other than Milan Lukic during your time in detention?" And in your answer, again, you did not mention Sredoje at all. Isn't it your statement under oath today?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I only saw Sredoje that once, and he only did that to me that once. Anything else would be a lie. But there is something I got from Spasojevic Milan or Mico Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Saban Murat Agic I got some from him too. Spasojevic took him along, and then they said --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered my question. I don't have any further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. A few re-direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, while you were in the detention camp, did you have a calendar with you, or was there a calendar in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: None in the camp, nor did I have anything on me to write. Once I left the camp, from Visoko to Sarajevo I started writing things down because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I just wanted to know about in the camp, okay? Did you have anyway of keeping track of the days that went by?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I had no way. I wasn't allowed to have anything, to keep anything. If there had been a policy in place, maybe we would have had music, newspapers, you know, but we had to leave everything outside the camp --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: -- our clothes, our shoes, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So are you able to tell us today the exact month that was the last time you saw Milan Lukic when he disappeared for a period of time and the exact month that he returned? Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 he showed up maybe twice, three times, perhaps, and then another time in 1993. So he was seen less and less as time went on. For two or three or four months he would be gone, and he wasn't to be seen anywhere around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you can't -- can you tell us today any -- and only if you remember, any of the months that you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, I don't know the month, he came with a revolver. He came to prison. He stood there right in front of me, and then the commander was their Commander Jelkic, who was the last commander for the guards there, and he sort of wanted to cover me with his own body just in case the man fired so he would go too. He wanted to protect me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, just -- the question is really a yes or no question. Do you remember the exact months --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Which months did you see Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994 when the most recent commander of the guards was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What month? Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether you remembered the month that you saw Milan Lukic. Do you remember the month that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can't take it any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, on -- you -- sir, there's no question before you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just a few more questions, sir. You did talk about seeing Sredoje once at the detention camp. Can you tell us if -- did he do anything to you and what -- and if he did, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And we already have answer, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think it was -- they confused the witness on cross-examination, Your Honour, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He answered that already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: He slapped me several times, hit me several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Witness, there's no question.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: And Milan was spurring him on. He said hit him, hit him harder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: But I didn't. You know, I can't say that he did. He just hit me several times. He slapped me across the face.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just a few more questions. While you were at the detention camp, sir, did you have any chores that you had to do?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? I was milking the cows.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: I was never taken back to town for maybe six months. You know, I took care of everything there. I would clean the prison up, tidy up, and then the facilities where we relieved ourselves, just to make sure that everything was clean when the Red Cross came.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: And then later, I -- we did some farming, and then out in our company and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So do you know if other detainees did any work outside of the barracks? In other words, would detainees leave sometime during the day and then return that same day later?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think this is a leading question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is partially leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, it isn't, Your Honour, because Mr. Dieckmann asked -- tried to establish that all of the pseudonymed persons were all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to reformulate it in a non-leading manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever see any of the detainees leave the barracks during the day and then return?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Come and go. They went out to work, they were divided in groups. It wasn't all just one group. There were several groups. One of them roughly speaking, a young man named Mirzet from Gostilje, named Bajic, Bajic Mirzet, and then he left with Saban, that one, you know which one I mean, Muratovic, and then they were off to do something, you know, and then they --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. No further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. -- I wanted to find out whether you have any evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Whether you have any evidence as to whether the conflict had any effect on this witness, any -- whether he's suffered any kind of injury or sustained any kind of a -- whatever kind of damage. Do you have any evidence as to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I did ask him on direct, Your Honour, what -- but he didn't provide details. I can ask him again if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe you might be able to get it independently, independently of him, from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If Your Honour requests that, we can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm interested if it is a result of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask him one further question about --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, are you currently taking medication?

utterances.speaker: NURKO DERVISEVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of September, 2008, at 2:15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
